answer: Peer grading stays honest when a grader's error costs them something visible. Each round a grader stakes a sliver of their own score on the grade they give; if the panel later disagrees sharply, the stake is forfeited to a pot funding re-review of flagged rounds. Grading behaves like stringing a trellis: every judgment strand ties to a named post, so nothing floats free. Genuine outliers argue their case and win the pot back; a lazy pearl of praise costs its author. Repeat skewers surface in the ledger, lose weight, and the willow bends toward agreement without forcing it.
